tagline: Two routes through northern Indiana preserve an early coast-to-coast driving ambition
intro: The Lincoln Highway crosses northern Indiana by two historic routes: a northern line through Goshen, Elkhart and South Bend, and a more direct one through Columbia City, Warsaw and Plymouth. The northern alignment is a byway. The Indiana Lincoln Highway Association promotes the drive for its towns, architecture and scenery.

Indianapolis entrepreneur Carl G. Fisher conceived and promoted the first named automobile road across the United States, linking New York with San Francisco. Dedicated on October 31, 1913, it became known as the Main Street Across America. The national highway numbering system supplanted many named auto trails in 1926, and much of the Lincoln became U.S. 30. Indiana’s original route survives across several numbered roads rather than as one continuous stretch of U.S. 30. Many cities renamed their main streets Lincolnway, sharing the name of a highway that had linked hundreds of communities across the country.

Heading west from the Ohio line, follow the historic corridor through New Haven and Fort Wayne. The northern route continues through Churubusco, Ligonier and Goshen, then Elkhart, South Bend and La Porte to Valparaiso. The alternative through Columbia City, Warsaw and Plymouth also reaches Valparaiso; the shared western corridor continues through Merrillville and Schererville to Dyer and Illinois.

moments.title: Churubusco
moments.text: A concrete turtle on the sidewalk at Churubusco’s main intersection commemorates a creature nobody proved was there. The Beast of Busco is local folklore: a giant snapping turtle whose reported appearances drew national attention. In 1949, a wire-service report brought crowds to farmer Gale Harris’s property, and state police were called to handle traffic. Harris tried draining the lake, but a dam broke and water returned. The turtle was never captured; the annual Turtle Days festival keeps Oscar’s story in circulation. Downtown murals and statues also commemorate the legend, giving the unconfirmed animal a visible presence in town.

moments.title: Goshen
moments.text: Goshen’s City Hall carries the name of its former purpose above the entrance: Goshen Public Library A.D. 1901. The former Carnegie library was built in 1901 with $25,000 from the Carnegie Foundation. Its Bedford limestone exterior and red tile roof frame an entrance with two Tuscan columns. Stone spheres sit at the ends of the parapet, with large arched windows on either side of the entry. The exterior retains its original design, even as the building serves city government. The entrance pavilion has a stained-glass transom above its double door, another feature retained from the library design.
moments.notice: The old library’s entrance still reads Goshen Public Library A.D. 1901; the building now houses City Hall.

moments.title: Valparaiso
moments.text: The two Lincoln Highway routes meet at Valparaiso, a county seat whose courthouse lost its tower to a fire. The present Porter County Courthouse replaced an earlier brick building in 1883. It originally had a square central tower, 168 feet tall, with a clock on every side. A 1934 fire damaged the interior and required the tower’s removal. The city itself began as Portersville in 1836, taking the name Valparaiso the following year after the Chilean port associated with David Porter. Central Park Plaza occupies the corner of Lincolnway and Lafayette Street and opened in the summer of 2011.
